NGA.hook: The most populous country in Africa — about one in six Africans is Nigerian — and Nollywood releases more films a year than Hollywood.
NGA.place: On the Gulf of Guinea at the inner corner of the West African bulge.
NGA.borders: Anglo-French and Anglo-German treaty lines of 1885–1906 boxing Britain's Niger trading sphere — cutting through Yoruba, Hausa and Kanuri lands alike; the oil-rich Bakassi peninsula was transferred to Cameroon by a world-court ruling, completed in 2008.

CIV.hook: Grows roughly 40% of the world's cocoa — more than the next two countries combined. Also answers to Côte d'Ivoire.
CIV.place: On the Gulf of Guinea between Ghana and Liberia.
CIV.borders: France's coastal colony lines of the 1890s: river stretches near the coast, then ruler lines inland — the eastern edge splitting Akan peoples with the British Gold Coast, today's Ghana.

GHA.hook: The first colony in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence, in 1957 — and Lake Volta is the largest reservoir on Earth by surface area.
GHA.place: On the Gulf of Guinea, between Ivory Coast and Togo.
GHA.borders: The Gold Coast plus British Togoland, which voted in a 1956 UN plebiscite to join Ghana — so the eastern border is the WWI partition line of German Togoland, still splitting the Ewe people with Togo.

BFA.hook: Its name was invented in 1984 and means land of upright people — stitched together from two different local languages.
BFA.place: Landlocked directly above Ghana and Ivory Coast, below Mali and Niger.
BFA.borders: Pure administrative convenience: France created Upper Volta in 1919, dissolved it in 1932 — dividing it among three neighbours — and reassembled it in 1947; independence froze the restored outline.

SEN.hook: Reaches the westernmost point of mainland Africa, and almost completely surrounds another country — The Gambia.
SEN.place: The Atlantic tip of the West African bulge, wrapped around The Gambia on three sides.
SEN.borders: France's oldest African colony, wrapped entirely around the British enclave of the Gambia — the inner border traces the river's banks at roughly gunboat range, nearly cutting Senegal in two.

GIN.hook: Holds the world's largest bauxite reserves — and the Niger, Senegal and Gambia rivers all rise in its highlands.
GIN.place: On the Atlantic below Senegal, between Guinea-Bissau and Sierra Leone.
GIN.borders: French Guinea's treaty lines of the 1880s–1900s against Portuguese Guinea, British Sierra Leone and Liberia — rivers and watershed stretches that give the country its curling hook around its smaller neighbours.

BEN.hook: The birthplace of Vodun, which is an official religion here — and home of the Dahomey kingdom's all-female regiment.
BEN.place: A narrow strip running north from the Gulf of Guinea, between Togo and Nigeria.
BEN.borders: Colonial Dahomey: a narrow corridor drawn northward from the coast between British Nigeria and German Togoland, splitting Yoruba lands in the east and reaching inland to the Niger river bend.

SLE.hook: Freetown sits on one of the largest natural harbours in the world, which is why freed slaves were resettled there in 1792.
SLE.place: On the Atlantic coast between Guinea and Liberia.
SLE.borders: A British freed-slave settlement at Freetown, expanded inland to lines agreed with France in 1895; the Liberian border along the Mano river separates it from the other freed-slave republic.

LBR.hook: Founded by freed American slaves in 1847, making it Africa's oldest republic — and more of the world's shipping flies its flag than almost any other.
LBR.place: On the Atlantic below Sierra Leone, west of Ivory Coast.
LBR.borders: Founded by American freed-slave settlers in 1822 and never colonized — but France and Britain trimmed its claimed hinterland through the 1880s–1900s to today's lines along the Mano and Cavalla rivers.

TGO.hook: One of Africa's narrowest countries — about 110km wide but 550km long, a strip you can drive across in two hours.
TGO.place: A thin ribbon between Ghana and Benin, running north from the Gulf of Guinea.
TGO.borders: The eastern strip of German Togoland: the colony was split after WWI, Britain's western strip eventually voting to join Ghana, France's eastern strip becoming Togo — a partition remnant 550 km long and barely 100 km wide.

GNB.hook: The Bijagós archipelago off its coast is 88 islands, only about twenty of them inhabited — and a biosphere reserve.
GNB.place: A small Atlantic country tucked between Senegal and Guinea.
GNB.borders: Portuguese Guinea's limits against surrounding French West Africa, set by an 1886 Franco-Portuguese convention — rivers and short survey lines around the stretch of coast Portugal actually held.

GMB.hook: The smallest country in mainland Africa — a ribbon of land either side of one river, nowhere more than 50km wide.
GMB.place: Following the Gambia river inland, enclosed by Senegal on every side but the Atlantic.
GMB.borders: Africa's strangest border: a ribbon along both banks of the Gambia river, agreed with France in 1889 at roughly ten kilometres per bank — by legend, the range of British gunboat cannon.

CPV.hook: Ten volcanic islands that were completely uninhabited until Portuguese ships arrived in 1456 — everyone there descends from later arrivals.
CPV.place: An Atlantic archipelago about 570km west of Senegal, out on its own.
CPV.borders: Uninhabited Atlantic islands when the Portuguese arrived in 1456 — the state's extent is simply the archipelago Portugal settled; its only boundaries are maritime.
